newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's de Silguy rejects speculation of EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: EU's de Silguy rejects speculation of EMU delay.

text.p: European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy strongly rejected on Thursday speculation that the start of economic and monetary union (EMU) could be delayed or the criteria for entry changed.
"There is no question about changing the criteria or changing the date," de Silguy told a briefing with Swedish journalists.
His comments come amid growing speculation that Germany's economic difficulties might prompt the need for a postponement of the EMU's 1999 start date.
But a Reuter poll of 45 analysts on Thursday showed 76 percent still expected a single European currency to be launched on schedule.
De Silguy, who will visit Stockholm on Friday, also said he expected several countries to be ready for EMU.
He referred to a Commission forecast last November projecting European Union 1997 growth at 2.3 percent and said there was no reason to believe the figure would be lower.

De Silguy said the only way of delaying EMU would be to change the EU treaty, but this could cause legal disputes, be negative for Europe's credibility and open the door for pressure groups in all member states regarding national budgets.
Financial markets have been rife with speculation of a delay to monetary union, with various theories being floated of how it might be managed.
One has EMU starting in 1999, in principle, but with no members. Proponents say this strategy would avoid a messy renegotiation of the Maastricht Treaty.

EU officials, however, have criticised the so-called empty shell strategy as not workable. The open-ended nature of such a plan would sow confusion in financial markets and slow down preparations in the private sector.

Regarding France's proposed stability council, an informal grouping of finance ministers that would discuss economic policy issues under EMU, de Silguy said such a body could be a good thing but should not interfere in the policies of the future European Central Bank (ECB).
"This council should remain very informal and should not in any circumstances interfere in the conduct of monetary policy which is the competence...of the European Central Bank," he said.
The idea came under attack earlier this year, notably from some members of Germany's Bundesbank who feared it might be used to determine the independence of the ECB.
At a bi-lateral meeting in Lyon, France on Wednesday, German and French officials reaffirmed their support for an informal stability council.
